1.2.3.15-r1.burton_quote: peculiar Fury, which comes by overmuch study

1.2.3.15-r10.burton_quote: Not a day that I spend idle, part of the night I keep mine eyes open, tired with waking, and now slumbering to their continual task

1.2.3.15-r11.burton_quote: saying, he came from hell as a Spy, to tell the devils what mortal men did
1.2.3.15-r11.translation: In the disguise of a Fury he went round the city, ... [to report] the sins [of mortals].

1.2.3.15-r12.burton_quote: I knew in my time many Scholars, saith Aeneas Silvius (in an Epistle of his to Gaspar Schlick Chancellor to the Emperor), excellent well-learned, but so rude, so silly, that they had no common civility, nor knew how to manage their domestic or public affairs. Paglarensis was amazed, and said his Farmer had surely cozened him, when he heard him tell that his Sow had eleven Pigs, and his Ass had but one Foal.

1.2.3.15-r13.burton_quote: privileges than the rest, that adventure themselves and abbreviate their lives for the public good

1.2.3.15-r14.burton_quote: King Hieron got more by Simonides’ acquaintance, than Simonides did by his

1.2.3.15-r16.burton_quote: Leaping (as he saith) out of our beds, when we hear the bell ring, as if we had heard a thunder-clap

1.2.3.15-r17.burton_quote: a good Philosopher as much excels other men, as a great King doth the Commons of his country

1.2.3.15-r2.burton_quote: puts Study, contemplation, and continual meditation, as an especial cause of madness

1.2.3.15-r3.burton_quote: Many men (saith he) come to this malady by continual Study, and night-waking, and of all other men, Scholars are most subject to it

1.2.3.15-r4.burton_quote: that have commonly the finest wits
1.2.3.15-r4.translation: and those of much forethought easily fall into melancholy.

1.2.3.15-r5.burton_quote: he had a Bible in his head
1.2.3.15-r5.translation: He became melancholic through too much study, saying that

1.2.3.15-r6.burton_quote: why Students dote more often than others
1.2.3.15-r6.translation: why their minds are troubled with constant melancholy and frequent ravings, so that they are driven out of their wits

1.2.3.15-r7.burton_quote: other men look to their Tools, a Painter will wash his Pencils, a Smith will look to his Hammer, Anvil, Forge: an Husbandman will mend his Plough-Irons, and grind his Hatchet if it be dull; a Falconer or Huntsman will have an especial care of his Hawks, Hounds, Horses, Dogs, &c.: a Musician will string, and unstring his Lute, &c., only Scholars neglect that Instrument, their brain and spirits (I mean) which they daily use, and by which they range over all the world

1.2.3.15-r9.burton_quote: which dries the brain and extinguisheth natural heat; for whilst the spirits are intent to meditation above in the head, the stomach and liver are left destitute, and thence come black blood and crudities by defect of concoction, and for want of exercise, the superfluous vapours cannot exhale
1.2.3.15-r9.translation: whence the brain becomes cold and dry, which is melancholic.
